why: Two implementations decide which forwarded hop is the client, and every
per-client control in the framework is keyed on the answer: the built-in
`rate` middleware, the server-action rate limiter, and the action replay
guard's per-client quota. The native host is
crates/ruvyxa_middleware/src/client_ip.rs and the deployed host is
`clientAddress` in packages/ruvyxa/runtime/serverless-handler.mjs.
They disagreed. `RateLimitLayer::extract_key` read the transport peer and
never looked at a forwarded header, so one project with one
`middleware.builtin.rate` block was limited per real client once deployed
and as a single shared bucket when the native server ran behind a reverse
proxy — every caller draining one counter, which turns the control meant to
protect the service into the thing that denies it.
The table starts *after* the trust decision about this request's own
upstream hop, the same way `trustedScheme` is an input to
origin-policy-conformance.json rather than something that table derives.
The native server believes a forwarded header only when the transport peer
is loopback or listed in security.trustedProxyIps. A deployed function has
no peer to weigh, so the adapter that emitted it declares which header its
own platform ingress writes and overwrites -- cf-connecting-ip on
Cloudflare, x-vercel-forwarded-for on Vercel -- through createHandler's
clientIpHeaders. Reading that list unconditionally is what the deployed
host used to do, and it was wrong on the standalone server the node, bun,
deno, aws, railway, and render adapters emit: that is an ordinary 0.0.0.0
HTTP server with no ingress writing anything, so the header was whatever
the caller typed and one client rotating it got a fresh bucket per
request. Those platform headers are therefore deliberately absent from
every case here.
Addresses are IPv4 only. Which hop is selected is the shared decision and
is what this table pins; how the selected address is spelled back out is
host-local — a bucket key never leaves the process that made it — and the
two hosts do format IPv6 differently. Each host covers IPv6 selection in
its own suite.
`client: null` means no hop could be attributed. The native host reports
that as None and falls back to the transport peer; the deployed host
reports the literal "unknown", which buckets more aggressively than the
traffic warrants — the direction a limiter is allowed to be wrong in.

cases.name: an empty forwarded header attributes nothing
a single hop is the client
surrounding whitespace is not part of the identity
the rightmost hop wins over a hop the client wrote itself
a forged run of hops cannot displace the one the proxy appended
a trusted proxy hop is skipped and the hop before it is the client
every trusted hop in a chain is skipped
loopback is a trusted hop without being configured
a chain of nothing but trusted hops attributes nothing
a bare address in the trusted list matches only that address
a bare address in the trusted list does not cover its neighbours
text that is not an address is not an identity
a header of nothing but junk attributes nothing
x-real-ip is read when x-forwarded-for is absent
x-forwarded-for is preferred when both are present
host bits outside a configured prefix do not narrow it
